questions.question: In an AS ABAP-based SAP system, you need to create a user that is not enabled for dialog interaction and is subject to the validity period of passwords. Which user type do you choose?
questions.why:
Dialog User: This user type is tailored for online access, suitable for RFC and background jobs. It's typically chosen when creating a user ID for an actual person.
System User: System users are designed for background jobs and RFC, excluding dialog logons (SAP GUI). They lack the capability to change their own passwords, requiring intervention from a user administrator. This user type is primarily intended for internal processes such as Transport Management System (TMS), Central User Administration (CUA), or Application Link Enabling (ALE). 
Communication User: Similar to system users (No Dialog Login), communication users serve background jobs and RFC. One important & unique point about communication users is, they can change their passwords themselves needing no manual intervention. 
Service User: Service users are dialog users aimed at accommodating a broader, anonymous user base, particularly useful when accessing the system anonymously via a web application. 
Reference User: Reference users function as templates for creating operational users with identical authorizations. Primarily encountered in the realm of internet users generated through Transaction SU01, a reference user lacks the ability to log on in any manner and cannot be utilized in background jobs.

Delta data backups: Picking up where it left off during differential or incremental data applications.
Log backups: Safely resuming during the replay of redo log backups via fallback checkpoints.

questions.question:
Using the Java Startup and Control Framework, what is the correct sequence of steps to start an application server of an AS Java-based SAP system?
1. Start Offline Deployment
2. Start bootstrap process
3. Start ICM/Server process(es)
4. Connect to SCS instance
questions.why: The Instance Controller first connects to the Central Services (SCS) instance, then runs offline deployment, then the bootstrap process (which synchronizes binaries and configuration from the database to the file system), and finally starts the ICM/server processes. That gives the order 4, 1, 2, 3.

questions.question: Which tools can you use to start an SAP system? Note: There are 2 correct answers to this question.
questions.why: An SAP system is started and stopped through the SAP Start Service (sapstartsrv). The SAP Management Console (SAP MC, a GUI) and SAPControl (a command-line tool used for scripting/automation) both drive that service. The Microsoft Service Manager and the ICM are not tools for starting an SAP system.

questions.question: Which service is located in each tenant database of an SAP HANA system?
questions.why: The index server is the core service present in every tenant database: it processes SQL/MDX statements and manages the actual data. The name server, compile server, and pre-processor server run on the system database (SYSTEMDB) and are shared across tenants, so they are not located in each tenant.

questions.question: What does SAP recommend you size before you install SAP HANA in a tailored data center integration (TDI). Note: There are three correct answers to this question.
questions.why: For a HANA tailored data center integration deployment SAP recommends sizing main memory (HANA is an in-memory database), persistent storage (data and log volumes, needed for durability and recovery), and IOPS (the storage must meet HANA's I/O performance KPIs). Network throughput and SAPS are not part of this TDI sizing recommendation.
